title: Frontend Testing Strategy
summary: A button appears simple, but users depend on its behavior across many situations.

subtopics.title: Unit tests
subtopics.explanation: A unit test checks a small piece of logic, such as a formatter or validation rule. It runs quickly and isolates one behavior. Use clear inputs and expected results, like checking a calculator with known sums. For example, a unit test can verify that a price formatter displays a zero value correctly. In a real page, a unit test can check that a date formatter handles a missing value.

subtopics.title: Component tests
subtopics.explanation: A component test checks what a user can see and do in one interface piece. It can click buttons, type text, and check accessible labels. Prefer user actions over implementation details. For example, a component test can submit an empty form and check the visible field error. In a real page, a component test can select a visible button by its accessible name. A component test is like rehearsing one scene with a real prop and actor.

subtopics.title: End-to-end tests
subtopics.explanation: An end-to-end test follows a real journey in a browser, such as signing in and saving a setting. These tests catch routing and integration failures but take longer to run. For example, an end-to-end test can sign in, change a preference, and reload the page. In a real page, an end-to-end test can cover checkout from cart through confirmation. An end-to-end test is like following a customer’s whole trip through a store.

subtopics.title: Test boundaries
subtopics.explanation: A test can replace a network service with a controlled response. This makes error and loading cases repeatable. Keep mocks near the boundary so tests still exercise the important UI behavior. For example, a controlled server response can reproduce a 500 error in a component test. In a real page, a mocked 500 response can verify that the UI offers a retry. A mock is like a controlled stand-in used to repeat one difficult situation.

subtopics.title: Risk and maintenance
subtopics.explanation: Test the behaviors most likely to harm users or break often. A few dependable tests are more useful than many flaky tests that teams stop trusting. For example, run stable checks in CI and quarantine flaky tests until their cause is understood. In a real page, remove flaky tests from the release gate until their timing is reliable. Test effort is like inspection time: spend more where failure would hurt most.

foundations.overview: Testing checks that important behavior keeps working after code changes. Unit tests check small functions. Component tests check interactions. End-to-end tests follow a user journey in a real browser. Choose tests based on risk, not on a target number.
foundations.mentalModel: A smoke alarm does not inspect every brick. It checks the failure that could put people in danger. Tests should focus on meaningful failures.
foundations.whyItMatters: A useful test gives the team confidence about a behavior users rely on. Choose the test level according to risk, feedback speed, and the boundary being verified.
foundations.browserPerspective: Frontend tests may run in Node, a simulated DOM, or a real browser; choose the environment that matches the behavior.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Test meaningful user paths and boundary cases such as slow responses, empty data, and failed submissions.
foundations.businessImpact: Good tests help a team ship changes confidently without slowing every small edit.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Use accessible queries so tests reflect how people find controls.
foundations.performanceImpact: Keep browser tests focused because they consume more time and resources.
commonUseCases: Test a formatter with a few known inputs and expected outputs.
Test a form by typing values, submitting it, and checking the visible error.
Test a complete browser journey when routing, storage, and network boundaries interact.
Check a high-risk form validation rule.
Verify a critical user journey across browser and API boundaries.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every function needs a separate unit test.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Prioritize meaningful user behavior and risky logic; excessive low-value tests add maintenance without protecting important outcomes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A passing component test proves the whole site works.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Component tests cannot cover every route, deployment setting, or real service; combine levels according to the risks.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Mocks make tests realistic by replacing everything.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Mocking too many boundaries can hide integration failures; keep critical behavior real in at least some tests.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More tests always make software safer.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Tests that assert implementation details or fail randomly can slow changes and reduce trust.

commonMisconceptions.myth: End-to-end tests should cover every tiny condition.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Use faster focused tests for detail and reserve browser journeys for high-value integration risks.

keyTakeaways: A unit test checks a small piece of logic, such as a formatter or validation rule.
A component test checks what a user can see and do in one interface piece.
An end-to-end test follows a real journey in a browser, such as signing in and saving a setting.
